newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan seen not high priority issue for China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan seen not high priority issue for China.

text.p: China is expected to step up pressure on Taiwan for reunification once it regains sovereignty over Hong Kong in mid-1997, but for now it has bigger fish to fry, a senior ruling Nationalist Party official said on Friday.

Director-general of the department of mainland affairs, Huang Yao-yu, said Taiwan was not high on Beijing's priority list of issues to be dealt with immediately after the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Deng died late on Wednesday at the age of 92.
"With the post-Deng power transition and Hong Kong handover ahead, Taiwan is definitely not on the list of urgent issues for the mainland," Huang told Reuters.
"But it's highly possible that the Taiwan issue will be one of the top agenda (items) at the mainland's 15th congress in October," he added.
The crucial party congress is due to approve China's political agenda into the 21st century.
Once Hong Kong returns to the motherland after 150 years of British colonial rule on July 1, China is expected to swiftly turn its attention to the Taiwan issue, local analysts said.

China hopes its principle of "one country, two systems," to be implemented in Hong Kong, can also be applied to Taiwan. Communist China has said Hong Kong can keep its system of freewheeling capitalism unchanged for 50 years.
Nationalist-ruled Taiwan and China have been political rivals since a civil war separated them in 1949.
Beijing views the island as a renegade province which it wants to eventually bring back into the mainland fold, threatening to take Taiwan by force if it opts for independence.
Relations across the Taiwan Strait plunged to news lows in March 1996 when Beijing held missile tests in waters near the island during Taiwan's first direct presidential elections.
The tests, meant as a warning to Taiwan not to renege on its official stance in favour of reunification, depressed financial markets on the island and sparked widespread nervousness.
Chinese President and Communist party chief Jiang Zemin, Deng's anointed heir, may take a tougher stance on Taiwan with an eye on Beijing's hardliners, Huang said.
Huang said his party believed some hardliners in China were not satisfied with Jiang. "Those hardliners think Jiang Zemin is too soft and not tough enough," he said.
Unlike Deng or his predecessor Chairman Mao Zedong, Jiang has no war or military experience, which impairs his standing with China's three million-strong army.

Jiang, who takes full power after Deng's death, is a technocrat and career communist with a sure grasp of Chinese politics but a personal history that has little in common with that of his revolutioary predecessors.

"When Deng was still alive, the hardliners might not complain that much because Deng was behind Jiang. But now Deng is gone, we must keep a very close eye on how Jiang deals with those hardliners when they discuss the Taiwan issue," he said.
Huang said the ruling party's China affairs department held intensive meetings after Deng died to analyse Taiwan-China relations during the post-Deng era.
The Taiwan government was prepared for all sorts of possibilities and would work hard to keep the peace with China, Huang said.
